title: The Spanish Digital Certificate: Who Can Get One, and What a Founder Abroad Does Without a NIE
excerpt: The UGE says you need an electronic certificate to file. The FNMT gives three ways to prove your identity for one, and every one of them asks for a DNI or NIE. What that means for a founder who has neither yet.
keyTakeaway: An FNMT natural-person certificate requires a DNI or NIE, in person at an accreditation office or a Spanish consulate, or by video identification. A founder outside Spain with no NIE files through a legal representative who holds a certificate.
summaryEn: What the FNMT and the Justice ministry publish about getting a Spanish digital certificate: the three identification routes, the documents each asks of a foreign citizen, and the consequence for an entrepreneur applicant who has no NIE yet.

faq.q: Can I get a Spanish digital certificate with only a passport?
faq.a: Not from the FNMT. Its identity page lists, for a foreign citizen, a Foreigner Identification Card showing the NIE plus passport, or the official document granting the NIF/NIE plus passport. The video route asks for a DNI or NIE number at the first step.

faq.q: Can a friend in Spain get the certificate for me?
faq.a: Only if your signature on the certificate contract has been legitimised before a notary first. The FNMT says a power of attorney is not accepted for this.

faq.q: Can I get the certificate at a Spanish consulate?
faq.a: Yes. The FNMT says identity for the citizen certificate can be accredited at Spain's career consular offices abroad. You still need the request code from the online step, and the office will ask for your identity documents.

content:
The first article in this series ended on the one thing you need before the Spanish entrepreneur permit can be filed: an electronic certificate. The UGE's page says so in as many words. This article is about the certificate itself, as the two authorities that issue and explain it describe it: the FNMT's "Acreditar identidad" page and the Justice ministry's page on video identification. Both were read on 8 November 2026. The point that matters most for a founder comes at the end, and it is not good news for everyone.

What the certificate is

The Fábrica Nacional de Moneda y Timbre (FNMT) issues the "certificado de persona física", the natural-person certificate most people in Spain use to sign and file with the administration. Getting one has four steps on the FNMT's own page: configure your computer, request the certificate online, prove your identity, download the certificate. The third step is where a foreign applicant either passes or stops.

Route one: an accreditation office in Spain

After the online request you receive a request code by email. You then go in person to an identity accreditation office. The FNMT says it has more than 2,400 of them across Spain, with an office locator on its site, and that offices of the tax agency, Social Security and some others require an appointment. It also says, in bold, that this certificate cannot be requested at Correos post offices. Once an office has accredited you, the download is available immediately and the FNMT advises downloading at once.

What a foreign citizen brings, in the FNMT's words:

  • the request code from the email, and
  • a Foreigner Identification Card (the red, green or white card) showing the NIE, together with the passport, or
  • the official document granting the NIF or NIE, together with the passport.

The FNMT adds that the NIE document is accepted whether or not it is still in date; what the office is verifying is that you hold the number. The applicant must be at least 18, or an emancipated minor, and the identity document must be the original and valid, or an officially certified copy.

Route two: a Spanish consulate abroad

The same page says that if you are abroad you can accredit your identity at Spain's career consular offices, and lists the consulates where the citizen certificate can be handled. Customs registries do not count. The document requirements do not change by moving the appointment to a consulate: the office is still checking a NIE or NIF document against a passport.

Route three: video identification

The Justice ministry's page describes a fully remote route. You install the FNMT configurator, start the request, and at the request step you enter the holder's DNI or NIE, first surname and an email address; the request code arrives by email and you set a password that will be asked again at download. For identification you enter the request code and a mobile number, confirm an SMS, scan a QR code with the phone, show both sides of your identity document to the camera, and record a video selfie with a liveness check. The FNMT then reviews the evidence and emails you when the certificate can be downloaded. Forget the password and you start again.

Notice the first field of the request: DNI or NIE. The remote route is remote, but it is not a way round the identity number.

If you cannot go yourself

The FNMT allows a third person to accredit your identity on your behalf, but with one condition: your signature on the certificate contract must first be legitimised before a notary. It then answers the obvious question on the same page: a power of attorney is not valid for this; what is required is the notarial legitimation of your signature. If you are planning to send someone, ask the FNMT's page, not a forum, what that person must carry.

The consequence for a founder abroad

Put the three routes together and the pattern is clear. Every route verifies a Spanish identity number. A founder who lives outside Spain and has never held a NIE is not the person any of these pages describes. That is why, in practice, the entrepreneur permit is so often filed by a legal representative: the law as amended in 2022 says the application is made by the applicant or through a legal representative, electronically, with the UGE. The representative's certificate signs; your documents are the content.

Two provisions of the 2022 Startups Law point the same way and are worth knowing. One says Spain will facilitate issuing the NIE to people applying under this law, with a dedicated web page for appointments. The other, added to article 76, says that for the first six months of residence a passport is enough to register with Social Security when the holder has no NIE yet. The first is a promise about the number; the second is a workaround for one specific use of it. Neither gives you a certificate before you have a number.

What to do with this

  1. If you already hold a NIE from an earlier stay or purchase, you can get the certificate yourself: online request, then an accreditation office in Spain or a consulate, or the video route.
  2. If you do not, decide early who your legal representative will be, and confirm that they hold a valid certificate. The filing in our Spain guide assumes exactly this.
  3. Do not pay anyone for "a certificate without a NIE". The FNMT's own page is the test: if the documents you have are not on its list, the office will not accredit you.

Whether Spain is the right file to open is a separate question, and the route finder answers it in a few minutes.
